title: Starling murmurations
hook: Thousands of starlings turn as one, and no bird is in charge.
peek: On winter evenings, huge flocks of starlings pour across the sky in shapes that fold and ripple like smoke. There is no leader. Each bird watches only a handful of neighbours, and the whole cloud emerges from that.
lede: On autumn and winter evenings, starlings gather before roosting and fly in vast, shifting clouds called murmurations. Flocks can number in the tens or hundreds of thousands, and the shape ripples and folds as if one mind were steering it. There is no leader. Research suggests each bird is mostly tracking a few of its nearest neighbours.

bullets.text: The word murmuration has been used for a flock of starlings since at least the 1400s, apparently for the soft rushing murmur of thousands of wings turning together.

A 2008 study in Rome filmed flocks in 3D and found that each starling responds to about six or seven nearby birds, whatever the distance between them. That keeps the flock together even as it stretches and thins.

Later work on the same Roman flocks found that a change of speed or direction passes from bird to bird across the whole flock with little fading. That is why a turn starting at one edge can sweep the entire cloud.

The leading idea is that the swirling makes it hard for a falcon or hawk to pick out a single bird. Murmurations often grow more dramatic when a predator is nearby, before the flock drops into its roost at dusk.
